youtube_title: Why Your Cruise Between U.S. Ports Stops in Another Country 🦝⚖️
caption: Under the Passenger Vessel Services Act regulations, a non-U.S.-qualified ship can sail a round trip from one U.S. port with a nearby foreign stop — but ending at a different U.S. port needs a distant foreign port.
script: Your cruise stops at a random foreign port because of a law from eighteen eighty six. [disclaimer] It's called the Passenger Vessel Services Act. It limits foreign ships, like most big cruise ships, from carrying passengers from one American port to another. Customs has rules that explain how it works. If a foreign cruise ship only visits American ports, and you get off at a different American port, that breaks the rule. Busted! Now add a quick stop nearby, like Canada, Mexico, the Bahamas, or the Caribbean. If you end the trip back at the same port where you got on, that's okay! That's one reason so many round trip cruises throw in a quick foreign stop. But if you end the trip at a different American port, a nearby stop isn't enough. The ship would need to go somewhere far away, outside that nearby list. And there are special cases too, like Puerto Rico. Here's the limit. A foreign stop doesn't make every trip legal. And this is the passenger rule. It's not the Jones Act rules for cargo. Cruise lines can ask Customs for an official answer, and nothing here means any certain route is approved. [loop] So the next time your cruise makes a surprise stop abroad, remember
